page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.d1.2xlarge is an instance in the Big Data series, built for data warehousing, distributed file systems, and bulk sequential storage workloads. It is powered by a dedicated Intel Xeon E5-2682v4 processor running at 2.5 GHz on the x86_64 architecture, providing 4 physical cores and 8 vCPUs via hyperthreading. The configuration features 32.0 GB of system memory, yielding a 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio of 4.0 GB per thread, alongside a baseline network throughput of 3 Gbps. Notably, the instance includes an integrated 23,622 GB local HDD storage array, while lacking dedicated GPUs.

Benchmark evaluations position the ecs.d1.2xlarge on the lower spectrum of general compute and memory speeds. The server scored 957.0 on single-core and 3,546.0 on multi-core Geekbench assessments, reflecting bottom 25% performance tiers. CPU results via stress-ng similarly placed in the bottom 25%, with 1,096.39 for single-core and 5,838.18 for multi-core. PassMark tests produced an overall CPU score of 7,009.91 and extended instructions performance of 5,848.19, both situated in the middle 50% band. Compression benchmarks demonstrated lower throughput, with single-threaded gzip compression at 18.75 GB/sec and single-threaded bzip3 decompression at 5.95 GB/sec, placing them in the bottom 10%. Memory read bandwidth on large 256 MB blocks yielded 37.11 GB/sec, while write bandwidth achieved 34.88 GB/sec.

The primary tradeoff of the ecs.d1.2xlarge revolves around its storage-heavy architecture versus legacy compute execution. Compute operations and memory access are constrained compared to modern architectures, evidenced by a PassMark database operations metric of 2,165.2 and Redis throughput reaching 5.63 million operations per second. However, cost efficiency is realized through dense, direct-attached spinning disk capacity, offering substantial local gigabytes per vCPU without external storage provisioning costs. The instance is suited for batch processing, secondary data analytics, data lakes, Apache Hadoop or Spark worker nodes, and large-scale sequential log archival where massive volume takes precedence over raw compute velocity.
